..
Issued at 325 PM CDT Tue Sep 1 2026

...Synopsis...

Yesterday's upper low has migrated into interior ON, with
increasing upper moisture/clouds from an approaching weak
shortwave trough in SD/NE. This weak shortwave to traverse
through SD into southern MN this evening into early Wednesday.
While some of its upper/mid level moisture will overspread our
area, dry air near the surface will prevent most rain from
reaching the ground out of the showers that attempt to develop
near the tri-state area this evening/tonight.

Wednesday will be dry with weak winds amid surface high 
pressure and decreasing cloud cover. 

Late Wednesday into Thursday, upper ridging begins to build 
into the Northern Plains downstream of a longwave upper trough 
digging into the Pacific Coast. This will promote moisture 
return into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest Thursday. 
This continues through the rest of this week as an omega-block
pattern sets up over the CONUS, with upper ridging further 
building into the Plains in response to the digging and non- 
progressive upper troughing in the West. This will allow 
several days of southwest flow aloft over the Northern Plains
(including our region), allowing for continued and somewhat 
lengthy period of moisture and heat return/reinforcement 
through the rest of this weekend. This will bring ingredients 
into the Northern Plains and Upper Midwest for potential severe
storms as well as summer-like heat with potential for minor 
heat related impacts.

Ensemble guidance suggests the upper trough and ridge wave 
packet breaks down into early next week, which typically would 
signal the end of heat and severe potential. However, there are 
notable difference between ensemble systems in how this 
breakdown evolves - thus confidence in the extended forecast is 
low.

...Potential strong to severe storms mid to late this week...

Most recent guidance has somewhat delayed the approach of the 
initial initial surge of southwest flow aloft to bring 
moisture/instability into our area compared to yesterday,
placing confidence in late Wednesday devoid of robust
thunderstorms. There still could be some elevated robust
convection capable of small hail early Thursday morning,
however.

Confidence has grown in the juxtaposition of moderate to strong
instability and moderate shear enough to introduce a Level 1 
out of 5 risk for severe storms Thursday over our entire area,
but by no means is this a confidence forecast. There are still 
important questions regarding degree of capping, sufficient
forcing for ascent, and storm mode/evolution that are yet to be
resolved confidently. However, there is a potential scenario 
that brings at least sufficient forcing to sustain robust 
thunderstorm development amid the instability/shear spacing that
could result in supercells within eastern ND Thursday
afternoon/evening. This includes potential for large hail
(perhaps very large) and tornadoes given rich low level moisture
and the potential for surface low helping low level shear - both
of which would be dependent upon mature discrete/semi-discrete
supercell modes. On the other hand, there are scenarios that
favor more linear storm mode favoring gusty winds as main
hazard, as well as a scenario that is generally devoid of robust
convection within our area altogether - hence, lowered 
confidence for Thursday.

With non-progressive pattern allowing overall increased low
level moisture, along with continued feed of steepened lapse 
rates aloft sourced from the Central Rockies, the potential for
strong to severe storms exists almost daily through the weekend.
This is backed by ML/AI guidance highlighting our region late 
Thursday through Saturday for severe potential.

It is worth noting this pattern could result in locally heavy 
rain and potential for flash flooding given the longer duration 
of moisture flow and an upper pattern that is non-progressive 
potentially allowing for several shortwave impulses to traverse 
through our region. Confidence in this is low, however, as there
are unknown mesoscale influences that are necessary for flash 
flooding yet to be correctly resolved by modeled guidance.

...Late summer-like heat this weekend...

Ensemble guidance continues to strongly suggest in strong upper
ridging into the Upper Midwest this weekend. This will promote 
increasing temperatures aloft, as well as the migration and 
pooling of moisture near the surface. This will not only allow 
opportunity for 90s back into the forecast, but also high 
humidity. As of now, Friday and Saturday look to be the days 
where these two may align to bring heat indices well into the 
90s, and perhaps into the low 100s (20 percent chance of 
occurring). While Saturday looks to be hottest within the 
forecast period, this could also extend into Sunday, although 
confidence is low in this.
